summary: Micronesia issues a free 30-day visitor entry permit on arrival to citizens of essentially every country, with extensions available once you are there. US citizens go further still: under the Compact of Free Association they may enter, live and work in the FSM without a visa.

passportValidity.text: Your passport should be valid for at least 6 months on arrival. FSM immigration is commonly reported to accept 120 days' validity beyond entry, but airlines apply the stricter six-month rule. Confirm with your carrier before travel.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.certificate: International Certificate of Vaccination or Prophylaxis
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever certificate is required only if you are arriving from, or have recently transited, a country with risk of yellow fever transmission. No vaccination is required for travelers coming directly from Guam, Hawaii, Japan or the Philippines.

source.name: Federated States of Micronesia — national government portal

travelInsurance.text: Insurance is not checked at the border, but hospital facilities across the four states are basic and serious cases are flown to Guam, Hawaii or Manila — travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage is strongly advised.

source.name: Federated States of Micronesia — national government portal

onwardTicket.text: Visitors entering on the 30-day permit must hold a confirmed onward or return ticket; airlines check this at check-in and immigration officers may ask to see it.

source.name: Federated States of Micronesia — national government portal

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published. Officers may ask how you intend to support yourself, and proof of accommodation on the island you are visiting helps.

source.name: Federated States of Micronesia — national government portal

declarations.name: FSM arrival and customs declaration
declarations.submitWindow: Completed on the aircraft or at the airport on arrival
declarations.text: A paper arrival/departure card and a combined customs and quarantine declaration are handed out on the inbound flight. There is no online system. Keep the departure portion in your passport until you leave.

source.name: Federated States of Micronesia — national government portal

currencyLimits.text: Cash and other monetary instruments worth USD 10,000 or more must be declared on arrival and departure.

notes: Biosecurity is taken seriously — fresh fruit, vegetables, plants, seeds and animal products are restricted or banned to protect island agriculture.
Firearms and ammunition may not be brought in without prior written permission from the state police authorities.
Each state sets its own rules on importing alcohol, and some outer-island communities are dry. Check locally before carrying drink between islands.

payments.text: The FSM uses the US dollar, but card acceptance is thin outside a handful of hotels and dive shops in Pohnpei, Chuuk, Yap and Kosrae. ATMs exist in the state capitals and do run out of cash. Arrive with dollars in small notes.

safety.text: Serious crime against visitors is rare and island communities are welcoming. The practical risks are alcohol-related trouble after dark, occasional theft from unlocked rooms, weak road lighting, and how far you are from advanced medical care.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Micronesia travel information

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to April is the drier, calmer stretch — best for diving Chuuk Lagoon's wrecks and Yap's manta rays. Rain falls year-round and Pohnpei is one of the wettest places on earth.

tips.text: The FSM is four states — Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei and Kosrae — spread over 2,700 km. Each has its own airport, customs of its own, and often only a few flights a week; plan island-hopping around the United Airlines "island hopper" schedule.
Land, reefs and even paths are privately owned, especially in Yap. Always ask permission before walking, swimming or photographing on someone's land, and never take stone money or artefacts.
Bring more US dollars in cash than you think you need. ATMs are limited to the state centers, cards are often declined, and there is no way to get money on the outer islands.
Chuuk's wreck dives are deep and the island hopper flights are frequent. Leave a full 24 hours between your last dive and a flight, and note that the nearest recompression chamber is off-island.
Thighs are considered far more revealing than shoulders in much of Micronesia — swimwear is for the water, and a sarong or long shorts is the respectful choice in villages and towns.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Micronesia?
faq.answer: Almost certainly not. Citizens of essentially every country are admitted without a visa and receive a free 30-day entry permit on arrival, provided they hold a passport valid well beyond the stay and an onward ticket. US citizens do not need a permit at all under the Compact of Free Association.

faq.question: What does the Compact of Free Association mean for US citizens?
faq.answer: Under the Compact, US citizens may enter the Federated States of Micronesia without a visa and may live and work there indefinitely, and FSM citizens have the same right in the United States. You still pass through immigration and need a valid passport, and local rules on employment and land ownership apply.

faq.question: Can I stay longer than 30 days in Micronesia?
faq.answer: Yes. The FSM Division of Immigration in the state where you are staying can extend the visitor entry permit, usually in 30-day increments up to a total of 90 days. Apply before the current permit expires and bring your passport, ticket and proof of funds.

faq.question: Do I need any vaccinations for Micronesia?
faq.answer: Only a yellow fever certificate, and only if you are arriving from or have transited a country with yellow fever risk. Routine vaccinations should be up to date; dengue outbreaks occur, so mosquito precautions matter more than paperwork.

faq.question: How do you actually get to Micronesia?
faq.answer: Almost everyone arrives on the United "island hopper" service that links Guam and Honolulu via Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae and Kwajalein, or on the Guam–Yap flights. Seats are limited and the schedule is thin, so book flights before locking in hotels.
